packet.prompt:
Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

reader: Codex isolated native-resolution reader (model version not exposed)
text:
UNVERIFIED IMAGE READING — PACKET 03

Image-only layout survey
Both images are upright as supplied. Each shows four narrow columns, grouped as two pairs across a central vertical fold. I call the columns A, B, C, D from left to right; this is a coordinate convention, not an assertion about textual sequence across the fold. The writing is brown, compact, highly abbreviated, and of broadly similar size throughout. There are tall initial strokes and occasional larger rounded opening letters, but I cannot securely identify a rubric or question heading. No distinct red rubric, running title, or systematic underlining is securely visible. Fine horizontal and vertical lines occur, but some are surface lines or ruling rather than textual emphasis. I cannot confidently distinguish a main text and commentary layer, or separate marginal/interlinear glosses. Extensive irregular brown staining, abrasion, small holes, and large edge losses obscure both images. Image 002 has especially severe losses and blotches in the middle and lower portions.

Method and isolation
I inspected the two complete images for layout, then examined the following genuinely native-pixel crops. Images are 7857 x 6396 (001) and 7896 x 6411 (002). Crop coordinates are Pillow rectangles (left, top, right, bottom), with origin at the upper left. Crops were saved as PNG and displayed with original detail; no resizing, rotation, sharpening, reconstruction, or contrast adjustment was applied.

Reading convention
The few readings below are deliberately fragmentary. Each numbered line is a physical text line counted from the first surviving line at the top of its own column in the full image, not from the crop. The filenames identify the image; letters identify the columns. An uncertain word is followed by ?. [illegible] represents an unread span of unspecified length. A combining bar approximates a visible abbreviation mark; expansions in parentheses are proposals, not additional visible letters. No word is supplied merely to make a sentence grammatical. These are NOT continuous established Latin sentences.

Coverage and limitations
The lower/middle crops were examined specifically to avoid relying on the faded top sections and to seek connected prose or transitions. None yielded a passage I can transcribe reliably. I have not printed speculative pseudo-Latin for those regions. Thus this reading does not establish a usable heading, question opening, citation chain, quotation, or sustained connecting-prose passage. In particular, isolated possible words above should not be treated as source-matching evidence without independent glyph verification.

The complete images were surveyed, but most of their text remains unread. The upper selected spans are contiguous physical lines, not quotations assembled across the page. There is no overlap between the listed native crops that duplicates a transcribed line. Parts of the extreme column edges and tall ascenders may be clipped by crops; the original whole images retain the available extent. Holes and stained areas must not be silently bridged. No deliberate deletion or interlinear insertion is securely identified; apparent horizontal strokes cannot safely be called cancellations.

The limitation is both preservation and my inability to resolve this highly abbreviated hand confidently, not absence of native image pixels. Another paleographical reader working from these native crops could plausibly improve the reading. Full-height native column strips, with adjacent overlap and explicit baseline numbering, would also help review line counts and search other regions; another downscaled whole-image view would not address the reading problem.
